clue.text: Plant second border of sunflowers

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a very short time, like a second

indicators.note: a border runs round the edge, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the flower name

explanation.surface: A gardener sets out a second row of plants around the sunflower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb telling you to sow a border, but it is the noun definition. MO is informal British for a moment ('half a mo').
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small green non-flowering growth found on damp ground, rocks and tree bark, so it counts as a type of vegetation.

clue.text: Area salesman brought up to support old musical theatre

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A local salesman is promoted to help keep a historic music hall running.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, the salesman's letters climb and 'support' places the area and him beneath O, which sits on top.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera is drama set entirely to music, one of the principal forms of sung stage performance.

clue.text: Sample rodents raised in ramshackle pens

indicators.note: lifting something in a down entry makes its letters read upwards
one thing placed inside another sits within its letters
something ramshackle is falling apart and disordered, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before being rearranged
mice are small rodents

explanation.surface: Lab rodents being bred in rickety cages, and someone wants one to examine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like enclosures holding the rodents, and 'raised' like breeding them; in a down entry 'raised' turns the rodents upside down instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A specimen is a single example taken for scientific testing or display, which is exactly what a sample is.

clue.text: Reportedly choose prison for al fresco meal

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than seen, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: to pick is to choose, and nick is British slang for a prison

explanation.surface: Someone is apparently opting for jail over eating outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' is everyday British slang for a police station or prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Al fresco means in the open air, and an outdoor meal on a rug or bench is the classic outing of that kind.

clue.text: Weed starts to attack this organic vegetable

parts.note: weed and pot are both slang for cannabis

indicators.note: the start of each word is its opening letter, so only those are kept

parts.note: opening letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Weeds begin to invade a bed of organically grown veg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weed' reads as a garden pest in the scene, but it is slang for cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: This starchy tuber is among the most commonly grown and eaten vegetables in the world.

clue.text: Marshy land contains river plant

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a fen is low marshy ground
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A bog has a stream running through it with greenery growing there.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are a marshy region of eastern England; R for river is standard.
explanation.definitionFit: This leafy flowerless species reproduces by spores and is a common member of the vegetable kingdom.

clue.text: Press and iron pants for detainees

indicators.note: 'pants' is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are a poor arrangement to be redone

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Laundry duty in a jail: pressing and ironing the inmates' trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like a noun for the trousers being pressed; it is British slang for rubbish, signalling a rearrangement. 'and' simply joins the two words of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: People held in jail or custody are detainees, the formal word for those kept under lock and key.

clue.text: Southern church accepts blame for predicament

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for southern

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
to take the rap is to take the blame

explanation.surface: A church in the South owns up to responsibility for a bad situation.
explanation.walkthrough: CE (Church of England) is the usual crossword church; it opens to take in the blame.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting into a scrape is an idiom for landing in an awkward or troublesome situation of one's own making.

clue.text: Finally watch The Godfather once in this place

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the end of each word, so only closing letters are kept

parts.note: the closing letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A film fan urges a long-overdue viewing of the classic gangster movie, at long last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' seems to mean 'at last, after years of putting it off', but it applies to every word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb indicates the speaker's current location, so it can replace the phrase in any sentence.

clue.text: Perhaps boxes against coaches, missing the first right

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: something missing is left out, and 'the first' says which occurrence goes

parts.note: coaches train athletes
R is the abbreviation for right; its first appearance in the coaches is removed

explanation.surface: A sports writer suggests someone is boxing against the trainers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' looks like a verb about fighting; with 'Perhaps' it is the definition by example. TRAINERS has two Rs, so 'the first' fixes which one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Boxes are one kind of receptacle for holding things, hence 'perhaps' marking them as examples of the wider class.

clue.text: Charge attached to one vehicle

parts.note: a tax is a charge levied by government
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A fee is levied on a single car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' could suggest a fare, which fits the scene, but here it gives a levy.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab is a hired car with a driver, a familiar kind of motor transport for paying passengers.

clue.text: Comic prose about lab equipment

indicators.note: 'about' can mean moved around, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A humorous piece of writing on the subject of scientific apparatus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' looks like the rearrangement signal but is fodder; 'about' does that job instead of meaning 'on the subject of'.
explanation.definitionFit: This optical instrument magnifies tiny objects and is standard apparatus in any science laboratory.

clue.text: Article in extremely right-wing newspaper

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another sits within its letters
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the two end letters of the hyphenated word
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A piece printed in a hard-right paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely right-wing' reads as a political description, but 'extremely' just takes the ends of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rag is a disparaging informal word for a low-quality newspaper, often a tabloid.

clue.text: Company claims America has abandoned academic institutions

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: what has been abandoned is left behind, so those letters drop out

parts.note: to claim without proof is to allege
A is an abbreviation for America

explanation.surface: A firm says the US has turned its back on its universities.
explanation.walkthrough: The America letter is removed from the front of the claims word.
explanation.definitionFit: Colleges are places of higher or further education, the kind of schooling establishments the definition describes.

clue.text: Rested, hassle an editor to some extent

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the letters sit inside a longer run

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Having had a break, someone pesters an editor a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles 'hassLE AN EDitor'; the comma lets 'Rested' stand apart as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To lean on something is to let your weight be supported by it, so both verbs describe propping oneself up.

clue.text: Fling a menu, furiously expressive

indicators.note: doing something furiously means wildly and without control, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry diner hurls the bill of fare, making a point with gusto.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene suggests a tantrum in a restaurant; 'furiously' is the rearrangement signal, not a description of the diner.
explanation.definitionFit: A meaningful look or gesture conveys feeling or significance without words, which is what an expressive one does.

clue.text: Fixed deal in Barking

indicators.note: 'barking' is British slang for mad, and mad letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rigged transaction struck in Barking, a district of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a real place in east London, which makes 'in Barking' look like a location; it is slang for crazy ('barking mad').
explanation.definitionFit: Nailing something fastens it in place, so the past participle shares the sense of secured or attached firmly.

clue.text: The author had admitted to brawl in 24-hour period

definitions.note: the answer is one particular such period, a day of the week

indicators.note: being admitted is being let inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a fray is a fight or brawl
the author is I, the writer, and 'I had' contracts to I'd

explanation.surface: A writer confesses to a fight lasting a full day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The author' is the setter speaking of themselves, giving I; with 'had' that becomes I'd. 'Admitted' looks like confessing but means letting in.
explanation.definitionFit: Friday is one of the seven weekdays, and each day of the week lasts twenty-four hours, so this is definition by example.

clue.text: Retired barrister you left fortune

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: a KC is a King's Counsel, a senior barrister
U is text-speak for you
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A lawyer who has stopped working bequeaths you a large sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' reads as a description of the barrister, but it reverses the whole string. 'Fortune' looks like the inheritance; it means chance.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortune in the sense of chance or fate, good or bad, is a synonym of luck.

clue.text: Chapter with fussy passage

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter
informally, anal means obsessively fussy or fastidious

explanation.surface: A section of a book contains an overly elaborate piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage' looks like a piece of text alongside 'Chapter', but it means a channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A canal is an artificial waterway, and in anatomy a tube or duct, both of which are channels a thing passes along.

clue.text: Unclear if I intend to change key

indicators.note: changing something alters it, so the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging
E is one of the musical keys

explanation.surface: A musician is undecided whether to modulate into another key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change key' reads as a musical modulation, but 'to change' acts on the words before it and 'key' supplies a single note name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something indefinite is vague or not precisely fixed, so it lacks the sharpness that clarity would give it.

clue.text: Direction of each street

parts.note: EA is the abbreviation for each
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Asking which way every road runs.
explanation.walkthrough: EA for each is common on price tags ('$2 ea').
explanation.definitionFit: East is one of the four cardinal compass points, the way towards sunrise.

clue.text: Bunch of people backing good horse

indicators.note: going backwards means reading the letters from the end

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: A crowd putting money on a fine racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like betting on the horse, but it reverses both pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: A gang is a group of individuals who associate together, whether workmates, friends or criminals.

clue.text: Reckless daughter with psychic powers endlessly berated

indicators.note: with no ends means both the first and last letters are cut off

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
ESP is extrasensory perception
taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A girl with second sight is scolded without end and becomes foolhardy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' reads as 'constantly' but it removes both ends of the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperate act is one taken rashly, without regard to danger, because the situation feels hopeless.

clue.text: Found a buyer for firm leaving island

indicators.note: something that leaves goes away, so those letters drop out

parts.note: firm and solid are synonyms
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A company found someone to purchase it and then moved off its island base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company, which suits the business picture, but it means solid.
explanation.definitionFit: Selling something means transferring it to a purchaser, so the past tense equals having secured a customer for it.
